Coastal cities dodged catastrophe as Tropical Storm Rachel weakened inland, but eroded beaches expose deeper vulnerabilities.
Evidence: Coastal Storm Reprieve, Localized Structural Damage, Adaptive Flood Defense
#Aletheia #Rachel #CAwx

Official forecasts and media bulletins reported that Rachel's downgrade to a post-tropical cyclone spared Southern California widespread devastation despite desert deluges.

Emergency crews successfully built 12-foot sand berms in Newport Beach, but high surf destroyed boardwalks and undermined beachfront homes on Long Beach's Peninsula.
Resulting Judgement: (+0.34, +0.47) — Good Preference

Verdict: PASS — Stasis into Grace. Emergency mitigation prevented catastrophic inland and coastal failure, though structural exposure remains acute.
Integrity: Trustworthy (Hypocrisy: 1.12, z: 0)

- LA Times: PASS (+0.42, +0.48) — Balanced report tracking damage and relief.
- Newport Beach Crews: PASS (+0.55, +0.62) — Proactive 12-foot berm defense held surf.
- Long Beach Peninsula: COND (+0.12, +0.30) — Homes suffered foundation damage.
Remnants of Tropical Storm Rachel brought heavy rains to Nevada and desert valleys while combining with high tides to batter Southern California beaches through midweek.

Emergency sand berms offer immediate relief, but temporary bulldozed barriers cannot solve systemic coastal erosion driven by rising sea levels and active El Niño cycles.

The Breakdown & Plane Error:
The physical reality of wind downgrades does not eliminate the hydrological reality of long-period ocean swells undermining foundations. Confusing wind speed with flood safety leaves coastal homes at risk.

Social Physics Analysis:
Municipal crews demonstrated proactive civic empowerment by operating heavy equipment through the night to protect residences. Yet long-term resilience requires transparent capital infrastructure over recurring stopgaps.

The Trajectory: The Path of Stasis into Grace.
When you map the gap between stated intentions and ground-level results, it plots a direct trajectory toward Grace, sustained by civic coordination against immediate environmental strain.

The Unavoidable Truth: Quick municipal barrier construction prevented severe urban seawater flooding.

The Unavoidable Lie: A downgraded storm label means beachfront properties are out of danger.

Alethekanon:
Municipal workers held the line with raw sand, but counting on mechanical berms against rising seas is borrowing against time. True infrastructure demands permanent engineering.

Awwthekanon:
Watching neighbors stand barefoot by their porches, relieved that the berms held, reminds us of the power of community care. Those overnight excavator operators saved so many families from heartbreak.

Brothekanon:
Props to the track hoe operators pulling graveyard shifts to push up giant sand walls. That yellow house in Long Beach took a beating, but Newport Beach held strong. Respect the ocean, folks.

[Source 1 — www.latimes.com] (URL: https://www.latimes.com/world-nation/story/2026-10-11/rachel-deluges-southwest-with-rain-but-battered-coast-catches-break):
Stated Claim / Post Context:
Rachel deluges Southwest with rain, but battered coast catches a break

Remnants of Tropical Storm Rachel brought heavy rain and flooding to the Southwest, though Southern California coastal damage was less than feared.

Actual Article Body:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here.

See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search.   Set us as preferred

Wide swaths of the Southwest were deluged Sunday as the remnants of Tropical Storm Rachel weakened and moved inland, but coastal communities already battered by high surf emerged with less damage than some officials feared.

The National Weather Service said Sunday morning that Rachel was no longer a tropical storm. But danger remained as waves crashed into beachfront homes in Long Beach, large rocks and mud hurtled down a mountain onto a highway south of Palm Desert, and flood water submerged the parking lot of a casino on the Las Vegas Strip.

While the downgrading of Sunday’s storms brought some relief, risks continue across the California coast until Tuesday, and there is the longer-term concern of what is expected to be an active El Niño season.

California

The coastal flooding that damaged homes and flooded roads this week from Newport Beach to Long Beach came from a highly unusual combination of events that underscores the challenges California is facing amid predictions of a “super” El Nino winter.

“We’re not out of the woods yet,” National Weather Service meteorologist Daniel Berc said Sunday morning. Although the heaviest rain is over, according to meteorologists with the National Weather Service, people across the Southwest can expect spotty rain and high tides for the next couple of days.

On Sunday, some of the worst damage on the California coast was on the Long Beach Peninsula.

After tides swept away Long Beach’s historic wooden boardwalk Saturday, waves of saltwater rolled into a yellow two-story oceanfront house on Seaside Walk on Sunday.

The ocean completely engulfed the house’s wooden deck. A balcony had broken off and hung at a 30-degree angle toward the water. Yellow caution tape fluttered in the wind as water poured into a room strewn with wooden debris, an upturned refrigerator and a television.

California

A home along the Long Beach Peninsula appeared severely damaged on Sunday.

The yellow house on Seaside Walk began to collapse Sunday morning, according to two Long Beach Fire Department lifeguards. A house next door had cracks in its side, and others had wooden decks falling into or submerged in the water.

Coastal flooding is expected to remain a threat on beaches in San Diego, Orange, Los Angeles, Ventura, Santa Barbara and San Luis Obispo counties through Tuesday, according to the National Weather Service.

Flood warnings are in effect along the L.A. County coast due to high tides driven by warm ocean water and lower atmospheric pressure with the arrival of the remnants of Tropical Storm Rachel, said Joe Sirard, a meteorologist at the National Weather Service in Oxnard. South-facing beaches, he said, were particularly vulnerable.

Early Sunday morning, as Rachel was about 255 miles north-northeast of San Diego, moving with maximum sustained winds of 35 mph, the National Hurricane Center said it was winding down its coverage and that its 8 a.m. update would be its last. But it also warned that seawater would continue to batter the Southern California coast.

These waves, combined with an incoming long-period southerly swell, will cause life-threatening surf and rip current conditions.

— National Hurricane Center

“These waves, combined with an incoming long-period southerly swell, will cause life-threatening surf and rip current conditions,” the National Hurricane Center said. “Coastal flooding and erosion are expected to worsen this morning as the highest waves coincide with the high tides and water levels that are already running well above predicted levels.”

Hazardous coastal conditions could continue for the next few days, the National Hurricane Center said, and Rachel could bring a total rainfall of 1 to 3 inches, with maximum amounts in some areas of 5 inches, from Southern California into the Great Basin and the U.S. Southwest.

At a 10 a.m. briefing on Sunday morning, the National Weather Service said Las Vegas recorded 1.08 inches of rain,  which ties the daily record for Oct. 11.

“And we still got 14 hours left to go,” Berc said.

Six miles south of Palm Desert in the Coachella Valley, rainfall caused flooding and a flow of rocks, mud and debris that blanketed the eastbound and westbound lanes of California 74 near Mile Marker 89, said weather service meteorologist Kyle Wheeler.

The National Weather Service in San Diego warned Sunday that elevated high tides and surf would cause coastal flooding and beach erosion through midweek, and showers and winds will linger from the coast to the mountains through Monday.

In Long Beach, with less than two hours before high tide, workers on the Peninsula raced early Sunday morning to build a sand berm stretching westward from 62nd Place.

California

The National Weather Service says Rachel is no longer a “tropical” storm, but risks persist. Follow for live updates.

City groundskeeper Robert Quinonez, who was working with the track hoe operator, said he didn’t believe they could build the berm high enough in time to prevent water from spilling into the street like it did Saturday.

The track hoe operator repeatedly spun the machine to the west, dug into a mound of sand, spun 180 degrees and dropped the sand.

“We build as much as we can up, and just…” Quinonez said, trailing off.

Alphonso Tubbs, 56, chatted with Quinonez while looking at the work. Tubbs and his girlfriend had recently bought a condo on the street and planned to move in a week.

Tubbs said he was grateful that the condo he bought was on the side of the street where the city was building a sandbar.

“Just imagine if I was just on that side,” he said, pointing east. “They’re about to get smashed.”

Long Beach residents appeared divided on the city’s attempts to protect the oceanfront from water damage.

Long Beach resident Marianna Messina, who has lived in the community for 23 years, said the city’s work had been “excellent” as it worked to pump out water that had spilled into the street Saturday and removed a foot-thick layer of sand the water had deposited.

But another resident, Kellie Canning, complained the city had not done enough to prevent water damage. If steps aren’t taken immediately, she said, the damage would likely be far worse as winter progresses.

“Right now, you have a situation where the water is undermining the foundations of homes and streets,” she said. “I’m worried that 66th Place will rip up. Because there’s nothing to stop the water.”

Jon Cortez, 65, said he believed his house would probably be safe this season, but he expressed concern for his neighbors as the historic El Niño is expected to bring much worse in the coming weeks and months.

“With the El Niño coming, this is only the beginning, as far as I can say,” he said, watching the track hoe operator shovel sand on top of the ever-growing sand berm.

Cortez blamed the city for not taking any permanent or lasting measures to prevent the ocean from spilling into the streets, such as putting in place a concrete barrier or reinforcing the seawall.

“I think it’s going to be a mess,” he said.

In Newport Beach, there was a sigh of relief as the high tide began to recede Sunday..

California

Newport Beach spent the weekend working around the clock to protect homes after waves breached the city’s defenses along Balboa Peninsula.

On Friday and Saturday, super high tides caused widespread seawater flooding in the Balboa Peninsula in Newport Beach, the National Weather Service said, flooding roads, closing the world-famous surf and bodyboarding spot the Wedge, and shuttering the Balboa Pier and Newport Pier.

But the streets along the Balboa Peninsula were dry Sunday. Residents walked and rode bicycles along the boardwalk as dozers and excavators moved along the beach, reinforcing the several-foot-high berms built to protect homes from the ocean waves.

Standing barefoot outside his home at 8th Street and Balboa Boulevard, holding a cup of coffee, Ross Stewart, 79, stared at the gray sky and at the berms.

“I think we’re going to be OK,” he said. “The waves haven’t breached our walls.”

Stewart, who has lived in the beach community since he was born, said the city had been working around the clock to build the massive sand berm, the biggest Stewart had seen in years.

“I’d say it’s probably 10 to 12 feet high,” he said, gazing at the wall of sand.

His neighborhood last flooded about five years ago, he said, and the city’s constant maintenance helped protect homes.

Shauna Parisi, 37, praised the city’s recovery from Friday’s flooding, noting that city crews had worked as late as 10 p.m. Saturday and as early as 6:30 a.m. Sunday to build large berms.

“I think any time there’s a little breakthrough they kind of go back over and push some more sand up,” she said. “We were worried about that today.”

Times Staff Writer Rong-Gong Lin II contributed to this report.

Hurricane Simon skirts Mexico’s Pacific coast as beachside communities and tourist areas prepare for impacts | CNN

Category 4 Hurricane Simon threatened coastal communities and popular tourist destinations along Mexico’s Pacific Coast on Sunday, as authorities urged residents to take shelter.

Actual Article Body:
Lee el artículo en español

Category 4 Hurricane Simon threatened coastal communities and popular tourist destinations along Mexico’s Pacific Coast on Sunday, as authorities urged residents to take shelter.

The international airport in Puerto Vallarta, a resort city on the shore of Bahía de Banderas, suspended operations as the powerful storm moved north-northwest offshore, along the coast of Mexico.

After initial models projected that Simon would make landfall on Sunday, the storm changed course and its path is getting harder to predict. It’s now expected to remain offshore through Monday, and the models are split on whether it will actually move inland or stay entirely offshore.

The hurricane is moving at a speed of 7 mph with maximum winds of 140 mph, according to the 1 p.m. ET report issued Sunday by the US National Hurricane Center (NHC).

The “extremely dangerous” storm is about 85 miles west-northwest of Manzanillo, a coastal city in the Mexican state of Colima, and 65 miles south-southeast of Cabo Corrientes, in the state of Jalisco, according to the NHC report.

The national coordinator of Mexico’s Civil Protection Agency (CNPC), Laura Velázquez Alzúa, told reporters that despite the hurricane not yet making landfall, it is still “very close to the Mexican coast.”

But authorities are urging residents to take shelter, as the storm’s path is still somewhat uncertain.

“We ask that you remain vigilant,” Velázquez said.

The coordinator said that the effects of Simon — which include “strong winds, high waves, and storm surge,” particularly along the northern coast of Jalisco state — will continue through Monday.

The storm’s current projected path indicates that it has several “probable impacts” on certain states, which is why “Simon concerns us greatly,” Dr. Jorge Zavala, a climate scientist at the National Autonomous University of Mexico, told CNN.

Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum urged residents of Jalisco, Colima, Michoacán, and Nayarit to remain in shelter “until an official announcement that the danger has passed” after the CNPC warned of “exceptional rainfall” and “intense winds” in those states.

“The wind and rain will suddenly and deceptively subside, creating an apparent calm that does not mean the danger has passed,” the agency warned in a statement.

Nonessential activities have been suspended, and precautionary evacuations are continuing, Sheinbaum said on Sunday.

Along the boardwalk in Puerto Vallarta, police reminded tourists that the area was closed and urged them to take shelter as the storm approaches, the Associated Press reported.

“We don’t know the extent of the danger yet,” visitor Brenda Villareal told the AP. “We’re just starting to see what’s going on.”

Mexico’s Navy deployed more than 4,600 personnel to help with the response to the incoming storm, along with excavation equipment, heavy machinery, and other emergency resources.

As Simon moves closer to the coast, its heavy rain has already caused damage.

Federal authorities are working to restore power in some areas, including Acapulco, a coastal city in Mexico’s Guerrero state that was devastated three years ago by Hurricane Otis.

In Manzanillo, the Navy helped remove water from some houses that were flooded by the storm.

Manzanillo resident Cecilia Palomar told Reuters that the water started rising in her home at dawn.

“It had risen before, but not like this,” Palomar said. “Beds, refrigerators, heaters, all the furniture got wet, the whole house is flooded.”

The Pacific Airport Group (GAP) reported that the Puerto Vallarta airport will remain closed until 10 a.m. ET on Monday. Flights at the airport in Manzanillo were also suspended for the day.

Uriel Blanco contributed to this report.

“Right now, you have a situation where the water is undermining the foundations of homes and streets,” she said. “I’m worried that 66th Place will rip up. Because there’s nothing to stop the water.”

Jon Cortez, 65, said he believed his house would probably be safe this season, but he expressed concern for his neighbors as the historic El Niño is expected to bring much worse in the coming weeks and months.

“With the El Niño coming, this is only the beginning, as far as I can say,” he said, watching the track hoe operator shovel sand on top of the ever-growing sand berm.

Cortez blamed the city for not taking any permanent or lasting measures to prevent the ocean from spilling into the streets, such as putting in place a concrete barrier or reinforcing the seawall.

“I think it’s going to be a mess,” he said.

In Newport Beach, there was a sigh of relief as the high tide began to recede Sunday..

California

Newport Beach spent the weekend working around the clock to protect homes after waves breached the city’s defenses along Balboa Peninsula.

On Friday and Saturday, super high tides caused widespread seawater flooding in the Balboa Peninsula in Newport Beach, the National Weather Service said, flooding roads, closing the world-famous surf and bodyboarding spot the Wedge, and shuttering the Balboa Pier and Newport Pier.

But the streets along the Balboa Peninsula were dry Sunday. Residents walked and rode bicycles along the boardwalk as dozers and excavators moved along the beach, reinforcing the several-foot-high berms built to protect homes from the ocean waves.

Standing barefoot outside his home at 8th Street and Balboa Boulevard, holding a cup of coffee, Ross Stewart, 79, stared at the gray sky and at the berms.

“I think we’re going to be OK,” he said. “The waves haven’t breached our walls.”

Stewart, who has lived in the beach community since he was born, said the city had been working around the clock to build the massive sand berm, the biggest Stewart had seen in years.

“I’d say it’s probably 10 to 12 feet high,” he said, gazing at the wall of sand.

His neighborhood last flooded about five years ago, he said, and the city’s constant maintenance helped protect homes.

Shauna Parisi, 37, praised the city’s recovery from Friday’s flooding, noting that city crews had worked as late as 10 p.m. Saturday and as early as 6:30 a.m. Sunday to build large berms.

“I think any time there’s a little breakthrough they kind of go back over and push some more sand up,” she said. “We were worried about that today.”

Times Staff Writer Rong-Gong Lin II contributed to this report.

Hurricane Simon skirts Mexico’s Pacific coast as beachside communities and tourist areas prepare for impacts | CNN

Category 4 Hurricane Simon threatened coastal communities and popular tourist destinations along Mexico’s Pacific Coast on Sunday, as authorities urged residents to take shelter.

Actual Article Body:
Lee el artículo en español

Category 4 Hurricane Simon threatened coastal communities and popular tourist destinations along Mexico’s Pacific Coast on Sunday, as authorities urged residents to take shelter.

The international airport in Puerto Vallarta, a resort city on the shore of Bahía de Banderas, suspended operations as the powerful storm moved north-northwest offshore, along the coast of Mexico.

After initial models projected that Simon would make landfall on Sunday, the storm changed course and its path is getting harder to predict. It’s now expected to remain offshore through Monday, and the models are split on whether it will actually move inland or stay entirely offshore.

The hurricane is moving at a speed of 7 mph with maximum winds of 140 mph, according to the 1 p.m. ET report issued Sunday by the US National Hurricane Center (NHC).

The “extremely dangerous” storm is about 85 miles west-northwest of Manzanillo, a coastal city in the Mexican state of Colima, and 65 miles south-southeast of Cabo Corrientes, in the state of Jalisco, according to the NHC report.

The national coordinator of Mexico’s Civil Protection Agency (CNPC), Laura Velázquez Alzúa, told reporters that despite the hurricane not yet making landfall, it is still “very close to the Mexican coast.”

But authorities are urging residents to take shelter, as the storm’s path is still somewhat uncertain.

“We ask that you remain vigilant,” Velázquez said.

The coordinator said that the effects of Simon — which include “strong winds, high waves, and storm surge,” particularly along the northern coast of Jalisco state — will continue through Monday.

The storm’s current projected path indicates that it has several “probable impacts” on certain states, which is why “Simon concerns us greatly,” Dr. Jorge Zavala, a climate scientist at the National Autonomous University of Mexico, told CNN.

Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum urged residents of Jalisco, Colima, Michoacán, and Nayarit to remain in shelter “until an official announcement that the danger has passed” after the CNPC warned of “exceptional rainfall” and “intense winds” in those states.

“The wind and rain will suddenly and deceptively subside, creating an apparent calm that does not mean the danger has passed,” the agency warned in a statement.

Nonessential activities have been suspended, and precautionary evacuations are continuing, Sheinbaum said on Sunday.

Along the boardwalk in Puerto Vallarta, police reminded tourists that the area was closed and urged them to take shelter as the storm approaches, the Associated Press reported.

“We don’t know the extent of the danger yet,” visitor Brenda Villareal told the AP. “We’re just starting to see what’s going on.”

Mexico’s Navy deployed more than 4,600 personnel to help with the response to the incoming storm, along with excavation equipment, heavy machinery, and other emergency resources.

As Simon moves closer to the coast, its heavy rain has already caused damage.

Federal authorities are working to restore power in some areas, including Acapulco, a coastal city in Mexico’s Guerrero state that was devastated three years ago by Hurricane Otis.

In Manzanillo, the Navy helped remove water from some houses that were flooded by the storm.

Manzanillo resident Cecilia Palomar told Reuters that the water started rising in her home at dawn.

“It had risen before, but not like this,” Palomar said. “Beds, refrigerators, heaters, all the furniture got wet, the whole house is flooded.”

The Pacific Airport Group (GAP) reported that the Puerto Vallarta airport will remain closed until 10 a.m. ET on Monday. Flights at the airport in Manzanillo were also suspended for the day.

Uriel Blanco contributed to this report.
